o: Describe how regular samples turn an analogue sound wave into digital data.
Calculate uncompressed mono sound size using sample rate, duration and bit depth.
Explain when lossy or lossless compression is appropriate.
c: Sound in the world is a continuous analogue wave. The revision booklet describes digital sampling as taking regular snapshots of the wave and recording each measurement as binary.
Sample rate counts samples taken per second. More samples can capture changes in the wave more accurately.
Bit depth controls the number of possible amplitude levels. Booklet mono formula: samples per second × duration (seconds) × bits per sample = bits; divide by 8 for bytes.
Lossless methods reconstruct original data exactly; lossy methods discard some information to achieve smaller files.

104.memoryCue: Booklet 'sound snapshots': sample rate = samples per second, duration = seconds, bit depth = bits per sample. Mono size (bits) = sample rate × duration × bit depth. Lossless restores EXACTLY; lossy removes data.

challenge.coreHint: Multiply the three sound factors before converting bits to bytes.

stretch.task: Modify Code First so it prints file size in bytes for 2 seconds at 2000 samples/s and 16-bit depth.
stretch.hint: sizeBits = sampleRate × duration × bitDepth; sizeBytes = sizeBits DIV 8.

mastery.task: Two mono recordings are the same duration. A is 8000 samples/s at 8 bits; B is 16000 samples/s at 16 bits. Calculate the ratio of their uncompressed sizes and explain the possible quality trade-off.
mastery.hint: Multiply rate × depth for each; the common duration cancels.
mastery.answer: A uses 64,000 bits each second and B 256,000 bits each second, so B is four times the uncompressed size. B can capture more temporal detail and amplitude precision; this does not guarantee a perceptible improvement in every case.
